name: Barceló-Visser Wormholes of a Conformally Coupled Scalar Field
description: Static, spherically symmetric traversable wormholes held open by a massless scalar field coupled to the curvature with the strength $1/6$, written down by Kirill Bronnikov in 1973 and found again by Carlos Barceló and Matt Visser in 1999 in a class with three parameters that also holds Schwarzschild's black hole and naked singularities. The effective Newton constant has opposite signs at the two ends of each wormhole, and the wormholes are unstable.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, with the Ricci tensor the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The length $\mu$ is half Barceló and Visser's $\eta$, and $b = \tan(\Delta/2)$ for their angle $\Delta$.
history: A massless scalar field coupled to the curvature with the strength $1/6$ has the stress tensor that particle physicists call the "new improved stress-energy tensor", and that tensor can break the null energy condition in classical physics [barcelo1999]. Carlos Barceló and Matt Visser, at Washington University in St. Louis, solved Einstein's equations with this field for static, spherically symmetric spacetimes and posted the solutions on 9 August 1999 [barcelo1999]. They found "a three-parameter class of exact solutions" that holds Schwarzschild's black hole, "assorted naked singularities, and a large class of traversable wormholes" [barcelo1999]. Barceló and Visser called the tensor an "inoffensive and physically well-motivated classical source" [barcelo1999].¶The stress tensor of the field has no trace, so the Ricci scalar of each of these spacetimes vanishes [barcelo1999]. Barceló and Visser multiplied the metric of the Fisher-Janis-Newman-Winicour solution, whose scalar field is minimally coupled, by a factor $\Omega^2$, required the Ricci scalar to vanish, and found a linear equation for $\Omega$ whose solutions have two constants, $\alpha_+$ and $\alpha_-$ [barcelo1999]. The class has three parameters, the length $\eta$ and the angle $\chi$ of the minimally coupled solution and an angle $\Delta$ with $\tan(\Delta/2) = (\alpha_+ - \alpha_-)/(\alpha_+ + \alpha_-)$ [barcelo1999]. At $\chi = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's, at $\chi = \pi$ it is Schwarzschild's with a negative mass, and at most other values the sphere $r = 2\eta$ is a naked curvature singularity [barcelo1999]. For $\chi$ between $0$ and $\pi/3$, with $\Delta \neq \pi/2$, the spheres grow without bound toward $r = 2\eta$, which lies at a finite distance, and Barceló and Visser called those wormholes "traversable in principle" [barcelo1999].¶At $\chi = \pi/3$ and $\Delta \neq \pi/2$ the areal radius and $g_{tt}$ tend to nonzero constants on $r = 2\eta$, and in an isotropic radius $\bar r$ the metric continues through that sphere [barcelo1999]. For $\Delta$ between $-\pi$ and $0$ the continued metric reaches a second asymptotically flat region as $\bar r \to 0$, with no horizon and a throat at $\bar r = (\eta/2)|\tan(\Delta/2)|^{1/2}$ [barcelo1999]. At $\Delta = 0$ the spheres shrink toward a smallest size at an infinite distance, a "tube without end" they called a "cornucopia", and for $\Delta$ between $0$ and $\pi$ the geometry closes at a finite radius [barcelo1999]. Across each wormhole the field $\phi_c$ runs monotonically from one asymptotic value to another, and the effective Newton constant $1/(8\pi(\kappa - \phi_c^2/6))$, with $G$ Newton's constant and $\kappa = 1/(8\pi G)$, has opposite signs in the two regions [barcelo1999]. Barceló and Visser proposed two thin shells of ordinary matter to join the wormhole at $\Delta = -\pi/2$, where $\phi_c^2 = 6\kappa$ everywhere, to two outer regions in which the effective Newton constant is positive [barcelo1999].¶Kirill Bronnikov had written the same metric down in 1973, as a special case of a family of static solutions for a conformally covariant scalar field in general relativity [bronnikov1973]. In Bronnikov's classification it is a space with a "neck" that leads to "another spatial infinity" [bronnikov1973]. Jan Frøyland solved the static, spherically symmetric equations for a massless scalar field with a traceless stress tensor in 1982, and Barceló and Visser described their class as a generalisation of Frøyland's solutions and of those A. G. Agnese and M. La Camera gave in 1985 [froyland1982, agnese1985, barcelo1999]. Bronnikov generalised the wormhole to conformal coupling in any number of dimensions in 1996 [bronnikov1996], and wrote in 2001 that it was "found for the first time" in the paper of 1973 and "recently discussed by Barcelo and Visser" [bronnikov2001conformal]. Bronnikov named the mechanism a conformal continuation, in which the conformal factor maps the singular centre of the minimally coupled solution to a regular sphere and the solution continues through it [bronnikov2001conformal]. The member of the same branch at $\Delta = 0$ is the black hole of N. M. Bocharova, Bronnikov, V. N. Melnikov, and Jacob D. Bekenstein, with the geometry of the extreme Reissner-Nordström black hole and a field that is unbounded on its horizon [bronnikov2001conformal, ray2025].¶Barceló and Visser extended the wormholes in 2000 to every positive coupling to the curvature, and showed that the field must reach values beyond the Planck scale somewhere in each of them [barcelo2000]. Bronnikov and S. Grinyok proved in 2001 that the wormholes are unstable under spherically symmetric perturbations, with a rate of growth that has no upper bound in linear theory [bronnikov2001instability]. The perturbation grows around the sphere where the effective Newton constant diverges and changes sign, and vanishes on that sphere itself [bronnikov2001instability]. Barceló and Visser wrote in 2002, citing Bronnikov and Grinyok, that their solutions are unstable [barcelo2002twilight]. Luke M. Butcher proved in 2015 that ordinary matter, in thin shells or spread out, cannot give a static, spherically symmetric wormhole of classical scalar fields a positive, finite effective Newton constant at both ends [butcher2015]. The matter the two shells would need breaks the null energy condition over a region of nonzero volume [butcher2015].¶Felix Willenborg, Saskia Grunau, Burkhard Kleihaus, and Jutta Kunz solved the geodesic equations of the wormholes in Weierstrass functions in 2018 [willenborg2018]. Stable bound orbits exist only on the side where the gravitational potential is larger, no bound orbit crosses the throat, and light has unstable spherical orbits at every finite angular momentum [willenborg2018]. Adolfo Cisterna, Keanu Müller, Konstantinos Pallikaris, and Adriano Viganò set a wormhole of the class in a rotating, swirling background in 2023, where it is dragged into rotation and acquires ergoregions [cisterna2023]. Sourya Ray showed in 2025 that the wormholes and the black hole of Bocharova, Bronnikov, Melnikov, and Bekenstein form one family of solutions with two parameters whose members are their own duals, with the black hole as its limiting case [ray2025]. Pablo Vidal found in 2026 that massless scalar waves on the wormhole depend on $\eta$ alone, so in four dimensions the wormhole and the extreme Reissner-Nordström black hole share the quasinormal frequencies of such waves [vidal2026].

related.text: The minimally coupled scalar field whose metric Barceló and Visser multiplied by a conformal factor $\Omega^2$ to reach these solutions, with Fisher's $b = 2\eta$ and $\gamma = \cos\chi$. The wormholes come from $\gamma = 1/2$ [barcelo1999].

One extremal charged hole with $m = \mu$, in isotropic coordinates. With its metric multiplied by $(1 - b\mu/\bar r)^2$ and $b < 0$, the solution is a wormhole of this class, and at $b = 0$ it is the geometry of the black hole of Bocharova, Bronnikov, Melnikov, and Bekenstein [ray2025].

Another wormhole of a massless scalar field, held open by a field whose kinetic energy is negative. Here the field has the ordinary sign and is coupled to the curvature, and the effective Newton constant changes sign across the throat [barcelo1999].
The general static traversable wormhole, whose throat needs matter that breaks the null energy condition. A classical field coupled to the curvature can be that matter [barcelo1999].

Matt Visser's wormhole of 1989, with all its matter in one thin shell. Barceló and Visser proposed two thin shells of ordinary matter to give these wormholes a positive effective Newton constant at both ends, and Luke M. Butcher proved that the shells would need matter that breaks the null energy condition [barcelo1999, butcher2015].
Friedmann universes of dust and the same conformally coupled field, which Barceló and Visser credited as the first sign that a classical scalar field can break the energy conditions [barcelo2000].

A black hole of three dimensions with a conformally coupled scalar field and a negative cosmological constant. In four dimensions with no cosmological constant the coupling $1/6$ gives these wormholes [barcelo1999].

Schwarzschild's black hole in a swirling universe. Adolfo Cisterna, Keanu Müller, Konstantinos Pallikaris, and Adriano Viganò set a wormhole of this class in the same rotating background in 2023 [cisterna2023].

coordinates.name: Isotropic, $\chi = \pi/3$

parameters.description: A length; far from the throat as $\rho \to \infty$ the metric is Schwarzschild's with $r_s = 2\mu(1 + b)$

A pure number, negative for the wormholes, whose throat is the sphere $\rho = \mu\sqrt{-b}$; the scalar field is $\phi_c = \sqrt{3c^4/(4\pi G)}\,(b\rho - \mu)/(\rho - b\mu)$, and $b = -1$ is the symmetric wormhole

coordinates.convention: We use Barceló and Visser's isotropic radius $\bar r$, written $\rho$, a length with $r = \rho(1 + \mu/\rho)^2$ on $\rho > \mu$ for their radius $r$, and $t$ having dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\dot{t}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

parameters.description: A length; far from $r = 4\mu$ the metric is Schwarzschild's with $r_s = 4\mu(\gamma + 2b\sigma)$
A pure number below 1, for which $\Omega$ is positive; the scalar field is $\phi_c = \sqrt{3c^4/(4\pi G)}\,\Psi/\Omega$
A pure number; $w = 0$ is Schwarzschild's black hole with $r_s = 4\mu$, and $w = 1/6$, where $\chi = \pi/3$, the branch of the wormholes
The exponent of Barceló and Visser's conformal factor, a pure number
Schwarzschild's function with $4\mu$ for $r_s$, a pure number

coordinates.convention: We use Barceló and Visser's radius $r$, a length, and $t$ having dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\dot{t}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$. Their angle $\chi \in [0, \pi)$ has $w = \tan(\chi/2)/(2\sqrt{3})$, so $\gamma = \cos\chi$ and $\sigma = \sin\chi/(2\sqrt{3})$.
